politeJa: 召し上がってください
use: Said by the cook at home as they serve, usually douzo meshiagare, often in reply to itadakimasu.

example.ja: はい、できたよ。どうぞ召し上がれ。
example.english: Okay, it's ready. Dig in.

examplePolite.ja: どうぞ、召し上がってください。

notes: Homey and a little playful; staff and formal hosts say meshiagatte kudasai instead.

kana: おかいけいおねがいします
use: Asks restaurant or bar staff for the bill; at many places you then pay at the register (reji) by the exit.

example.ja: すみません、お会計お願いします。
example.english: Excuse me, could we get the bill?

notes: Okanjou onegai shimasu is also common at izakaya.

english: two people; a table for two
use: Answer at the restaurant door when staff ask nanmeisama desu ka? (how many?).

example.romaji: futari desu. kauntaa demo ii desu.
example.ja: 二人です。カウンターでもいいです。
example.english: Two of us. The counter's fine.

notes: One is hitori desu, three is sannin desu. Holding up fingers works too.

use: Groaned after a big meal; half complaint, half compliment to the cook.

example.ja: あー、食べ過ぎた。お腹いっぱい。
example.english: Ugh, I ate too much. I'm stuffed.

examplePolite.ja: おいしくて、食べ過ぎました。
examplePolite.english: It was so good I ate too much.

politeJa: 持ち帰りでお願いします
use: Answer at a cafe or fast-food counter when staff ask if you're eating in (tennai de omeshiagari desu ka?).

example.ja: これ、持ち帰りで。
example.english: This one to go.

examplePolite.ja: 持ち帰りでお願いします。

notes: Staff say omochikaeri; chains also use teikuauto.

kana: べつべつでおねがいします
use: Asks to pay separately at the register; staff may ask goissho de yoroshii desu ka? (together?).

example.romaji: okaikei wa betsubetsu de onegai shimasu.
example.ja: お会計は別々でお願いします。
example.english: We'll pay separately, please.

notes: Splitting the total evenly among friends is warikan.

use: Called out at home, usually by a parent, to get everyone to the table.

example.romaji: minna, gohan da yo! hayaku kite.
example.ja: みんな、ご飯だよ！早く来て。
example.english: Everyone, food's ready! Come quick.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan desu yo. douzo suwatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯ですよ。どうぞ座ってください。
examplePolite.english: The meal's ready. Please sit down.

notes: Gohan means a meal as well as cooked rice.

english: what shall we eat?; what are you having?
use: Asks a friend what they want for a meal or what they're ordering.

example.ja: 昼ご飯、何食べる？ラーメン？
example.english: What should we have for lunch? Ramen?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no hirugohan, nani tabemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日の昼ご飯、何食べますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you having for lunch today?

notes: With a menu in hand, nani ni suru? (what are you getting?) is just as common.

politeJa: 好き嫌いはありますか
english: anything you don't eat?; are you picky?
use: A host or friend asks before cooking or ordering; answer tokuni nai (nothing really) or name the food.

example.romaji: kyou wa uchi de tsukuru kedo, suki kirai aru?
example.ja: 今日はうちで作るけど、好き嫌いある？
example.english: I'm cooking tonight. Anything you don't eat?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika suki kirai wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か好き嫌いはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Is there anything you don't eat?

notes: For allergies say arerugii ga arimasu.

politeJa: 冷めないうちにどうぞ
use: Urges someone to start eating or drinking now; usually followed by douzo or tabete.

example.ja: ほら、冷めないうちに食べて。
example.english: Come on, eat it while it's hot.

examplePolite.ja: 冷めないうちにどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: Please, have it before it gets cold.

notes: -nai uchi ni means before something happens: kuraku naranai uchi ni (before it gets dark).

english: to eat in, please; for here
use: Answer at a cafe or fast-food counter when asked if you're eating here; the opposite is mochikaeri de.

example.ja: 店内で、アイスコーヒー一つ。
example.english: For here, one iced coffee.

use: Casual invitation to eat out with a friend or coworker; the ni is dropped.

example.ja: 今度の土曜日、ご飯行かない？
example.english: Want to get something to eat this Saturday?

examplePolite.ja: よかったら、今度ご飯行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you're free, would you like to get a meal sometime?

notes: Kondo gohan ikou ne can be a vague pleasantry rather than a real plan.

kana: おすすめはなんですか
use: Ask staff at a restaurant or shop; casual version is osusume wa?

example.romaji: sumimasen, osusume wa nan desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、おすすめは何ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, what do you recommend?

notes: Menus mark recommended dishes as osusume.

politeJa: 大盛りでお願いします
use: Asks for an extra-large serving of rice or noodles, often for a small extra charge.

example.ja: 牛丼一つ、大盛りで。
example.english: One beef bowl, large.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan wa oomori de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯は大盛りでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: A large serving of rice, please.

notes: Normal size is namimori; a smaller one is sukuname.

use: Said when you're full and someone offers more.

example.ja: ごめん、もう食べられない。お腹いっぱい。
example.english: Sorry, I can't eat any more. I'm stuffed.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう食べられません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I couldn't eat another thing.

notes: Many speakers drop the ra: mou taberenai.

use: The toast that starts the drinking; wait until everyone has a glass before the first sip.

example.ja: じゃあみんな、お疲れさま！乾杯！
example.english: Okay everyone, good work today! Cheers!

examplePolite.ja: では皆さん、乾杯しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well, everyone, let's raise a toast.

notes: At work dinners someone usually gives a short toast speech first.

kana: ちゅうもんいいですか
use: Calls staff over when you're ready to order; start with sumimasen!

example.ja: すみません、注文いいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can we order?

notes: Many places have a call button on the table instead.

use: Asks staff for water; it's free, and some places have you pour it yourself (serufu saabisu).

example.ja: すみません、お水二つください。
example.english: Excuse me, two waters, please.

politeJa: とりあえずビールお願いします
use: The classic first order at an izakaya so the group can toast quickly; food comes after.

example.ja: みんな、とりあえずビールでいい？
example.english: Beer to start for everyone?

examplePolite.ja: とりあえずビール三つお願いします。

notes: Toriaezu alone means for now: toriaezu ikou (let's just go for now).

use: Staff's reply when they take your order or request; no answer needed.

example.ja: かしこまりました。少々お待ちください。
example.english: Certainly. One moment, please.

notes: At work you can say it to a boss or client; wakarimashita is the everyday version.
